History and Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
– Telehealth consultation with a 33-year-old engineer for 2–3 days of worsening wheeze and exertional shortness of breath; impression is an acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by viral illness and/or seasonal allergens.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Wheeze and shortness of breath.  
• Onset/duration: Began 2–3 days ago; progressive.  
• Character/progression: Wheeze, dry cough; dyspnoea on exertion (unable to walk to work, occasionally cannot finish sentences). No chest pain. No haemoptysis. Denies nocturnal awakening. Symptoms improve at rest.  
• Associated features: Self-reported “fever,” but measured 37 °C. No sputum production.  
• Triggers/relievers: None specifically identified; clinician suggested possible pollen or viral trigger. Uses salbutamol inhaler intermittently with partial relief.  
• Pertinent negatives: No smoking history, no chest pain, no night-time symptoms, no hospitalisation this episode.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – childhood onset, previously severe (occasional hospital visits). Off regular therapy for last 3–4 years; uses salbutamol PRN.  
• Hay fever.  
• Eczema.  
• No other chronic conditions reported.

Medications:
• Salbutamol inhaler, dose/route/frequency not documented (patient estimates use every few weeks and before exercise).  
• No other regular medications.  
Allergies:
• Denies drug allergies.

Social History:
• Lives with partner.  
• Occupation: Engineer; currently working from home or on sick leave due to dyspnoea.  
• Smoking: Never.  
• Alcohol: ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
Vitals: Temperature 37 °C (self-reported). No other vitals recorded.  
Examination findings: Not recorded (telehealth consultation).

Investigations:
• None performed today.  
• Planned: Peak-flow meter (home monitoring).

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
– Acute asthma exacerbation, likely precipitated by viral upper respiratory infection and/or seasonal allergen exposure.

DDx Integration (concise):
1. Acute asthma exacerbation – history of asthma, classic symptoms, exertional limitation; high likelihood.  
2. Viral respiratory tract infection with reactive airway – short duration, dry cough; possible trigger.  
3. Allergic (pollen-induced) asthma flare – atopic background supports, though fever less typical.

Issue 1 – Acute asthma exacerbation  
Assessment: 2–3-day flare with exertional dyspnoea; no red-flag features (no chest pain, normothermic, can climb stairs).  
Plan:  
• Increase salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours PRN.  
• Prescribe spacer; pharmacist to demonstrate correct technique.  
• Prescribe peak-flow meter; patient to record readings morning and evening for 1 week.  
• Start regular oral antihistamine (OTC; specific agent per pharmacist advice).  
• Safety-net: If temperature rises, wheeze worsens, or breathlessness at rest develops, call GP service urgently.  
• Follow-up: Telephone review in 1 week with peak-flow diary; consider addition of maintenance inhaler (e.g., inhaled corticosteroid) based on results.

Issue 2 – Atopic conditions (hay fever/eczema)  
Assessment: Under-treated hay fever may contribute to airway hyper-reactivity.  
Plan: Reinforce daily antihistamine use; reassess need for further allergy management at follow-up.

Issue 3 – Preventive asthma care  
Assessment: No current asthma action plan or regular preventer inhaler.  
Plan: Arrange comprehensive asthma review after acute episode to establish action plan, consider spirometry, and initiate long-term controller therapy if indicated.

General plan items:  
• Provide education on inhaler/spacer technique.  
• Encourage avoidance of known respiratory irritants/allergens.  
• Document peak-flow targets once baseline established.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: Objective vitals (HR, RR, SpO₂, BP) and physical lung examination not possible via telehealth.  
• Medications list incomplete for dose/frequency.  
• Family history not obtained.  
• No contradictions between transcript and DDx noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; occasional minor inaudible words but clinical content intact.

document_quality: acceptable
